sections.title: Omitting the agent; factual writing; informal contexts
sections.content:
We typically use a passive rather than an active in the following situations.
☆ Using a passive allows us to omit the agent (= the subject of the corresponding active sentence) by leaving out the prepositional phrase with by. We prefer passives when the agent:
- is not known: My office was broken into when I was on holiday.
- is 'people in general': An order form can be found on page 2.
- is unimportant: He is thought to be somewhere in Russia.
- is obvious: She is being treated in hospital. (the agent is clearly 'medical staff')
☆ In factual writing (e.g. describing procedures or processes) we often omit the agent, and use passives:
• Nuclear waste will still be radioactive even after 20,000 years, so it must be disposed of very carefully. It can be stored as a liquid in stainless-steel containers which are encased in concrete. The most dangerous nuclear waste can be turned into glass which will be stored in deep underground mines.
☆ In informal contexts, particularly in conversation, we often use active sentences with a subject such as people, somebody / someone, something, they, we, or you even when we do not know who the agent is. In more formal contexts, we often prefer to use a passive so that we can avoid any mention of an agent. Compare:
• They're installing the new computer system next month. and
• The new computer system is being installed next month. (more formal)

sections.title: Verbs with related nouns
sections.content:
Note also that some verbs have related nouns which express the same meaning. These nouns can be used as the subject of passive sentences, with a new passive verb introduced. Compare the example above and:
• The installation of the new computer system will be completed by next month.

sections.title: Topic and comment
sections.content:
In English we usually prefer to put the topic (what is already being talked about) at the beginning of a sentence (or clause) and a comment on that topic at the end. Choosing the passive often allows us to do this. Compare these two texts and note where the topic (in italics) is placed in the second sentence of each. The second text uses a passive where the emphasis is on the (safety) valves:
• The three machines tested for the report contained different types of safety valve. The Boron Group in Germany manufactured all the valves.
• The three machines tested for the report contained different types of safety valve. All the valves were manufactured by the Boron Group in Germany.
Using the passive allows us to put long subjects at the end of a sentence. So, for example:
• I was surprised by Dev's decision to give up his job and move to Sydney.
is more natural than 'Dev's decision to give up his job and move to Sydney surprised me', although the choice can depend on considerations of style and context.

sections.title: it-clause vs that-clause
sections.content:
Instead of making a that-clause the subject of a passive sentence, it is normal to use an it-clause (see also Unit 25):
• Everybody believed (that) the plan would fail. (active)
• It was believed that the plan would fail. (passive) is more natural than
• That the plan would fail was believed by everybody.

exercises.question: They built the main stadium in under three years. (Start: The main stadium...)
options: The main stadium was built in under three years.
The main stadium were built in under three years.
The main stadium had been built in under three years.
The main stadium builds in under three years.
exercises.hint: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: The main stadium was built in under three years.
Past simple passive: was/were + past participle. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: They have designed the main stadium to accommodate many different sports.
options: The main stadium has been designed to accommodate many different sports.
The main stadium have been designed to accommodate many different sports.
The main stadium were designed to accommodate many different sports.
The main stadium has been design to accommodate many different sports.
exercises.hint: Present perfect passive: has/have been + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: The main stadium has been designed to accommodate many different sports.
Present perfect passive: has/have been + past participle. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.sentence: The bridge was build in 1895 by a team of Scottish engineers.
exercises.correction: The bridge was built in 1895 by a team of Scottish engineers.
exercises.hint: Passive: was/were + past participle — 'build' is irregular, past participle = 'built'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was built
The passive voice uses 'be + past participle'. Many irregular verbs have distinct past participle forms: build → built, write → written, know → known, break → broken, speak → spoken. Using the past simple form ('build' or 'built' after 'was') is a common error.

exercises.question: They will take down the temporary stands after the Games.
options: The temporary stands will be taken down after the Games.
The temporary stands will taken down after the Games.
The temporary stands would be taken down after the Games.
The temporary stands being taken down after the Games.
exercises.hint: Future simple passive: will be + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: The temporary stands will be taken down after the Games.
Future simple passive: will be + past participle. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.question: They will have completed the basketball arena by the end of May.
options: The basketball arena will have been completed by the end of May.
The basketball arena will be completed by the end of May.
The basketball arena will have completed by the end of May.
The basketball arena would have been completed by the end of May.
exercises.hint: Future perfect passive: will have been + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: The basketball arena will have been completed by the end of May.
Future perfect passive: will have been + past participle. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.sentence: The report has been wrote by the finance department.
exercises.correction: The report has been written by the finance department.
exercises.hint: Present perfect passive: has/have + been + past participle. Write → written.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has been written
Present perfect passive: has/have + been + past participle. 'Wrote' is the past simple of 'write', not the past participle. The past participle is 'written'. This error is common with irregular verbs — it is worth learning: write/wrote/written.

exercises.question: They are holding the rowing competition on the River Nene.
options: The rowing competition is being held on the River Nene.
The rowing competition are being held on the River Nene.
The rowing competition is being hold on the River Nene.
The rowing competition was being held on the River Nene.
exercises.hint: Present continuous passive: is/are being + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: The rowing competition is being held on the River Nene.
Present continuous passive: is/are being + past participle. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: They had completed the athletics track only a year after the city got the Olympics.
options: The athletics track had been completed only a year after the city got the Olympics.
The athletics track have been completed only a year after the city got the Olympics.
The athletics track were completed only a year after the city got the Olympics.
The athletics track had completed only a year after the city got the Olympics.
exercises.hint: Past perfect passive: had been + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: The athletics track had been completed only a year after the city got the Olympics.
We use the past perfect here because this action happened before another past event.
💡 Past perfect passive: had been + past participle.

exercises.sentence: The concert is hold every year in July.
exercises.correction: The concert is held every year in July.
exercises.hint: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle. Hold → held (not 'hold').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is held
Present simple passive: is/are + past participle. 'Hold' is irregular — past simple and past participle are both 'held'. 'Is hold' uses the base form, which is wrong in the passive. Common irregular passives: is held, is told, is sold, is found, is known, is thought.

exercises.question: They will consider the issue at next week's meeting. (Use noun 'Consideration' and verb 'give')
options: Consideration will be given to the issue at next week's meeting.
Consideration will given to the issue at next week's meeting.
Consideration is being given to the issue at next week's meeting.
Consideration would be given to the issue at next week's meeting.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Consideration will be given to the issue at next week's meeting.
Future passive: will be given. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.question: They will appoint a new managing director next week. (Use noun 'appointment' and verb 'make')
options: The appointment of a new managing director will be made next week.
A new managing director appointment will be made next week.
The appointment for a new managing director will be made next week.
An appointment will be made for a new managing director next week.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: The appointment of a new managing director will be made next week.
Future passive with related noun. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.prompt: Transform this active sentence into the passive:
exercises.hint: Passive: subject + was/were + past participle + by + agent
exercises.explanation:
Answer: The vaccine was discovered by a scientist
Passive structure: the object of the active verb (the vaccine) becomes the grammatical subject. The agent (a scientist) follows 'by' at the end. Active: 'A scientist discovered the vaccine' → Passive: 'The vaccine was discovered by a scientist'.

exercises.question: They demolished the building in only two days. (Use noun 'demolition' and verb 'complete')
options: The demolition of the building was completed in only two days.
The demolition for the building was completed in only two days.
Demolition of the building was completed in only two days.
The building demolition was completed in only two days.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: The demolition of the building was completed in only two days.
Past passive with related noun. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: Slowly but surely the coastline of Britain ___ (wear away) by an advancing sea.
options: is being worn away
is wearing away
is worn away
was being worn away
exercises.hint: Present continuous passive: is/are being + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is being worn away
Present continuous passive: is/are being + past participle. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: experts ___ that this is just the beginning.
options: fear
are feared
have feared
is feared
exercises.hint: Active voice: the experts themselves are doing the fearing.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: fear
Active voice: the experts themselves are doing the fearing.

exercises.question: It ___ that there will be a 38-55 cm rise in average sea levels by the year 2100.
options: is estimated
estimates
was estimated
has estimated
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is estimated
Passive voice (it-clause): is + past participle. Choose the passive form that matches the tense and aspect of the active version.
